reading.body:
CyrusOne's Houston campus is the largest data center in Texas that publishes a power figure, at 84 MW, and it holds 18 percent of the state's disclosed IT capacity.

That share is a fact about disclosure, not about Texas. The state has 133 mapped data center facilities, and only 19 publish IT capacity, totaling 475 MW. The remaining 114 publish no power figures, so the full state capacity is unknown and the 84 MW campus ranks first only among the facilities that say how much power they draw.

IT load is the input that converts to compute. At 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, 84 MW across HOU3 and HOU4 supports roughly 2,100 racks. At 10 kW per GPU, it could feed about 8,400 high-end accelerators if fully allocated to GPU compute. Those figures are arithmetic on stated densities, not published configurations. The 347,000 square feet of technical space is the building envelope, and the 84 MW is what power can deliver into it. The Green Globes certification covers energy efficiency operations, not AI workload specificity.

What the data does not cover is the binding question. Whether this site's grid connection supports sustained AI training loads is not published. The suitability score of 77 is a weighted mean of published IT capacity and operator type, with announced expansion listed as missing. Nothing here states that the campus is allocated to AI compute at all, only that its disclosed power is large enough to matter at the state level.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
